analogy.p: Linear search is like looking for one letter in an unsorted pile by turning over every page from the top until you spot it: simple, but slow if the pile is huge. Binary search is like finding a name in a phone book or dictionary: you open the book in the middle, see whether your name comes before or after, throw away the half that cannot contain it, and repeat on the half that is left. With a thousand pages you need only about ten openings. The analogy breaks down because a person can jump to roughly the right letter and an actual computer must always start at the exact middle; and it only works because the book is already in alphabetical order, whereas the pile of papers is not.
analogy.t: Linear search is flicking through a stack of papers; binary search is a phone book

bullets: Input: a list (stored in an **array**) and a **target** value; output: the **position (index)** of the target, or a message or value showing it was **not found**.
Both algorithms use **iteration** (loops), **selection** (a comparison inside the loop) and **comparisons** with ==, <, >.
They are called **standard** algorithms because the same method is used again and again in many programs.
The spec asks you to know **how they work, their advantages and disadvantages, and when each is suitable**, not just the steps.
Link to other topics: the list is usually an **array** (indexes start at 0) and sorting algorithms (bubble, merge, insertion) produce the sorted list that binary search needs.
Remember to **always give a reason**: marks are for explaining why, e.g. 'binary search is faster because it halves the number of items each time'.
core.h: What searching algorithms do and why we need them
core.p: A **searching algorithm** finds out whether a particular value, called the **target** or search item, is in a collection of data and, if it is, where. Searching is one of the most common jobs a computer does: looking up a contact, finding a product in a database or checking a username. OCR J277 requires you to know two **standard searching algorithms**, **linear search** and **binary search**, to be able to describe how each works, apply it to a set of data, trace it, complete or write it in pseudocode, and compare their advantages and disadvantages. The key idea is that the best choice depends on whether the data is **sorted** and how **large** it is.

bullets: Step 1: start at the **first item** (index 0).
Step 2: **compare** the current item with the target.
Step 3: if they are **equal**, the target is found: stop and report the position (or True).
Step 4: if not equal, **move on to the next item** and repeat from step 2.
Step 5: if the **end of the list** is reached with no match, report that the target is **not found**.
The search can **stop early** once the target is found; there is no need to check the remaining items.
The order of the items does not matter, because every item is checked in turn, so linear search works on **unsorted data**.
core.p: A **linear search** (also called a sequential search) checks every item in the list one at a time, in order, starting at the first item, until it finds the target or reaches the end of the list. It is the simplest searching algorithm and it works on **any list, whether it is sorted or not**. At each step the item being looked at is compared with the target; if they are equal the search stops and reports where it was found, otherwise the search moves on to the next item. If every item has been checked without a match, the target is not in the list. Fig 1 shows a search for 25 that takes five comparisons.

bullets: function linearSearch(list, target) / for i = 0 to list.length - 1 / if list[i] == target then / return i / endif / next i / return -1 / endfunction.
**list.length - 1** is the last index, because indexes start at 0 (a list of 8 items has indexes 0 to 7).
**return -1** after the loop means 'not found'; it is only reached if no earlier return happened.
Flag version: set found = false and i = 0; **while i < list.length AND found == false**; if list[i] == target set found = true, else add 1 to i; after the loop use found to decide the output.
Common errors: looping to **list.length** instead of list.length - 1, which goes past the end; using = instead of ==; forgetting to **increase the counter** in a while loop.
Trace: searching [14,7,31,2,25,9,40,18] for 25 compares 14, 7, 31, 2, 25: **5 comparisons**, found at index 4.
Trace: searching the same list for 5 compares all **8** items and returns -1.
core.p: A linear search is naturally written with a loop that visits every index of an array. In OCR Reference Language a **for** loop runs from index 0 up to the last index, which is the length of the list minus 1, and an **if** statement compares the item at each index with the target. If a match is found the function returns the index straight away, which ends the loop and the function. If the loop finishes with no match, a value such as **-1** is returned to show the target is not there (a negative index can never be a real position). You may also see a version using a **while** loop and a Boolean flag; both are correct.

bullets: **Advantage**: works on **unsorted** data, so no time is spent sorting first.
**Advantage**: simple, short and easy to code and to test.
**Advantage**: efficient enough for **small lists**, or when you only need to search once.
**Disadvantage**: **slow for large lists**, because the number of checks grows in step with the number of items.
**Best case**: target is the first item: 1 comparison.
**Worst case**: target is last or missing: **n comparisons** for a list of n items.
Doubling the size of the list **doubles** the worst-case number of checks (Fig 4).
Exam phrase: 'it may have to check every item in the list, so it is slow for large data sets'.
core.h: Linear search: advantages, disadvantages and efficiency
core.p: Linear search is popular because it is very simple to understand and write, and because it does not need the data to be in any particular order. However it can be slow for large lists, because in the **worst case** (the target is the last item or is not in the list at all) every single item has to be checked. In the **best case** the target is the very first item and only one comparison is needed. On average, if the target is in the list, about half the items are checked. For a list of 1 000 000 items the worst case is a million comparisons, which is why linear search is a poor choice for very large collections.

bullets: **Pre-condition: the list must be sorted.** Without order, the target could be on either side of the middle, so half the list could not be discarded.
Each step **halves** the number of items still to be searched, which is why it is so quick.
It is a **divide and conquer** style method: split the problem, discard the half that cannot contain the answer.
The same method works on numbers (smallest to largest) and on text sorted alphabetically.
Link to other topics: if the list is not sorted, first use a **sorting algorithm** (bubble, merge or insertion sort).
Real-world analogy: finding a word in a **dictionary** by opening near the middle and deciding whether to go forwards or backwards.
core.h: Binary search: the requirement and the idea
core.p: A **binary search** is a much faster method, but it only works if the list is **already sorted** (for example in ascending order). Instead of checking items one by one it repeatedly looks at the **middle item** of the part of the list that is still possible. If the middle item is the target, the search is finished. If the target is smaller than the middle item it must be in the **left half**, and if it is larger it must be in the **right half**, so the other half can be thrown away completely. This halving is repeated until the target is found or there is nothing left to search. Because the amount of data is halved with every comparison, even a huge list needs only a few steps.

bullets: Step 1: set **low = 0** and **high = last index**.
Step 2: calculate **mid = (low + high) DIV 2**.
Step 3: if list[mid] == target, **found**; stop.
Step 4: if list[mid] < target, the target is in the right half: **low = mid + 1**.
Step 5: if list[mid] > target, the target is in the left half: **high = mid - 1**.
Step 6: repeat from step 2 while **low <= high**; if low > high, the target is **not found**.
For a list with an **even number** of items there are two middle items; DIV picks the lower one, and most mark schemes accept either as long as the method is clear and consistent.
Note the +1 and -1: the middle item has just been checked, so it is excluded from the next search.
core.p: To carry out a binary search by hand, keep track of the **low** index (the first item still possible) and the **high** index (the last item still possible). At the start low is 0 and high is the last index. Each time, calculate the **midpoint** as (low + high) DIV 2, where DIV means whole-number division that ignores any remainder. Compare the item at the midpoint with the target. If equal, you are done. If the middle item is smaller than the target, set low = mid + 1 because everything up to and including mid is too small. If the middle item is larger, set high = mid - 1 because everything from mid upwards is too big. Repeat until the item is found or low becomes greater than high, which means the target is not in the list.

bullets: Step 1: low 0, high 10, **mid 5**, item 31, 31 < 47 so **low = 6**.
Step 2: low 6, high 10, **mid 8**, item 52, 52 > 47 so **high = 7**.
Step 3: low 6, high 7, **mid 6**, item 40, 40 < 47 so **low = 7**.
Step 4: low 7, high 7, **mid 7**, item 47 = target: **found at index 7**.
After step 1 the search space shrank from 11 items to 5 (indexes 6 to 10); after step 2 to 2 items; after step 3 to 1 item.
A linear search for 47 would check 3, 8, 12, 19, 25, 31, 40, 47: **8 comparisons**, twice as many.
In a trace table the columns are **low, high, mid, list[mid]** and the result of each comparison.
core.h: Worked example of a successful binary search
core.p: Take the sorted list [3, 8, 12, 19, 25, 31, 40, 47, 52, 60, 71], which has 11 items at indexes 0 to 10, and search for 47. First low = 0 and high = 10, so mid = 10 DIV 2 = 5 and the item is 31. Since 31 is less than 47 the target is to the right, so low becomes 6. Next mid = (6 + 10) DIV 2 = 8, the item is 52, which is greater than 47, so high becomes 7. Then mid = (6 + 7) DIV 2 = 6, the item is 40, less than 47, so low becomes 7. Finally mid = (7 + 7) DIV 2 = 7 and the item is 47, which is the target. It is found at index 7 after only **4 comparisons**; a linear search would have needed 8 (Fig 2).

bullets: function binarySearch(list, target) / low = 0 / high = list.length - 1 / while low <= high.
Inside the loop: mid = (low + high) DIV 2 / if list[mid] == target then return mid / elseif list[mid] < target then low = mid + 1 / else high = mid - 1 / endif / endwhile / return -1 / endfunction.
The condition **low <= high** is crucial: using < would skip the case when only one item is left.
If low = mid + 1 or high = mid - 1 is written wrongly (e.g. low = mid) the loop may **never end** because the range stops shrinking.
The **while** loop is condition-controlled: we do not know in advance how many halvings are needed.
Flowchart: Start, set low and high, test low <= high, calculate mid, test equality, test less than, update low or high, loop back.
The function **returns the index** if found and -1 if not, so the calling program can output a suitable message.
core.h: Binary search in pseudocode and as a flowchart
core.p: In OCR Reference Language binary search is written with a **while** loop that continues as long as low is less than or equal to high. Inside the loop the midpoint is calculated and an **if / elseif / else** structure decides between the three possibilities: the item is found, the target is in the right half, or the target is in the left half. After the loop, a return value of -1 means the target was not found. The flowchart in Fig 3 shows the same logic: the diamond **low <= high ?** is the loop condition, and the two boxes that change low and high both lead back up to it.

bullets: The stopping condition **low > high** means the search range is empty.
Always include an **else/not found** outcome in your algorithm; missing it loses marks.
Searching for a value **smaller than every item** ends with high = -1 or low > high after moving left each time.
Searching for a value **larger than every item** ends with low past the last index.
A linear search for the missing 50 would need **11 comparisons**, so binary search is again quicker even when the item is absent.
In an exam trace, finish by writing clearly 'not found' or returning -1; do not leave the final result unstated.
core.h: Binary search when the target is not in the list
core.p: A good algorithm must also handle the case where the target is missing. In a binary search the range of possible items keeps shrinking, and when there are no items left, which happens when **low becomes greater than high**, the loop ends and the algorithm reports that the target is not found. For the same sorted list, search for 50. The sequence is mid = 5 (31, too small, low = 6), mid = 8 (52, too big, high = 7), mid = 6 (40, too small, low = 7), mid = 7 (47, too small, low = 8). Now low = 8 and high = 7, so low > high and the loop stops: 50 is not in the list, after 4 comparisons.

bullets: 8 items: linear worst case 8 checks; binary worst case **4** checks.
1000 items: linear **1000**; binary **10**.
500 items: binary needs at most **9** (500, 250, 125, 62, 31, 15, 7, 3, 1: halving until one item remains, then the last check).
Because binary search discards half of the remaining items each time, its work grows **very slowly** as the list gets bigger.
But binary search only wins if the list is **already sorted**; sorting a big list takes time too.
Best case for both: the target is the first (linear) or middle (binary) item: **1 comparison**.
core.p: The big difference between the two algorithms is how the number of comparisons grows as the list gets longer. For linear search the worst case is **n comparisons** for n items, so 1000 items could need 1000 checks. For binary search each comparison halves the remaining items, so the worst case is the number of times you can halve n before reaching 1, plus the final check. The maximum number of comparisons is the number of halvings needed: a list of 1000 items needs at most **10**, because 2 to the power 10 is 1024; a list of 1 000 000 items needs at most **20**, because 2 to the power 20 is 1 048 576. Doubling the size of the list adds only **one** extra comparison for binary search, but doubles the work for linear search (Fig 4).

bullets: Linear advantage: **works on unsorted data**; simple; good for small lists.
Linear disadvantage: **slow on large lists** (may check every item).
Binary advantage: **much faster on large lists**, with only a few comparisons.
Binary disadvantage: **list must be sorted first**; more complex to program.
If an unsorted list is searched **once**, linear search is usually quicker overall than sort-then-binary-search.
If the same list is searched **many times**, sorting once then using binary search is more efficient.
Data that changes often (many insertions) needs re-sorting, which makes **binary search less convenient**.
Exam tip: always mention **both** the size of the data and whether it is sorted when justifying a choice.
core.h: Choosing the right search: advantages and disadvantages
core.p: Choose by looking at the data. If the list is **small** or **unsorted**, linear search is usually the better choice, because it needs no preparation and is simple and reliable. If the list is **large** and **already sorted**, or will be searched many times, binary search is far more efficient. Sorting an unsorted list just to search it once is normally not worth the extra time, but if the same list will be searched again and again, sorting it once and using binary search each time pays off. Binary search is also a little harder to write and to understand, and a mistake in the low and high updates can cause errors or an infinite loop.

bullets: Always **calculate mid with DIV**, giving a whole number: (0 + 10) DIV 2 = 5, (6 + 7) DIV 2 = 6.
Count carefully: a successful search on the 4th check is **4 comparisons**, not 3.
Common bug in given code: **low = mid** instead of mid + 1, or **high = mid** instead of mid - 1, which can cause an infinite loop.
Common bug: loop condition **low < high** instead of low <= high, which misses the final item.
Common bug: looping a linear search to **list.length** instead of list.length - 1, which causes an index error.
Check the list is **sorted** before applying binary search; if not, say it cannot be used.

Link to other topics: sorting algorithms, arrays, iteration and selection, subprograms (functions that return an index), and testing with normal, boundary and erroneous data (first item, last item, missing item).
core.h: Tracing and exam skills for searching algorithms
core.p: Searching questions in Paper 2 usually give a short list and ask you to carry out a search by hand, complete a trace table, fill in missing lines of pseudocode, or spot an error in a given algorithm. For binary search always write down **low, high, mid and list[mid]** on every pass; this shows your method and protects you from arithmetic slips. Check that the list is in order before starting, because a question may deliberately give an unsorted list to see whether you notice that binary search is **not suitable**. When asked how many items are checked, count the comparisons with the target, including the successful one. You may also be asked to write or correct code, so learn the two pieces of pseudocode in this note thoroughly.

exam: **State/Name (1 mark)**: e.g. 'Linear search' or 'Binary search'; know that binary needs **sorted data**.
**Describe linear search (2 to 3 marks)**: 'start at the first item (1), compare each item with the target in turn (1), stop when found or the end is reached (1)'.
**Describe binary search (3 to 4 marks)**: sorted list (1), compare with the **middle item** (1), discard the half that cannot contain the target (1), repeat until found or none left (1).
**Apply an algorithm (2 to 4 marks)**: show every comparison; for binary search list the middle item each time and say whether the target is higher or lower.
**Why is binary search unsuitable? (1 to 2 marks)**: 'the list is not sorted, so you cannot tell which half the target is in'.
**Compare the two (up to 6 marks)**: include sorted vs unsorted, speed on large lists (fewer comparisons), simplicity of linear search, and a final judgement linked to the scenario.
**Trace table (3 to 4 marks)**: columns low, high, mid, list[mid]; update the right variable each row; finish with the output.
**Complete/correct code (1 to 3 marks)**: watch the loop condition (low <= high), mid + 1 and mid - 1, and the return -1 line.
**Count the comparisons**: include the final successful comparison; the first item takes 1, not 0.
Use phrases such as 'halves the list each time', 'must be in order', 'may have to check every item', 'fewer comparisons'.
For 'which search is most suitable' questions, always give a **reason that links to the data given** (size, sorted or not).

mistakes.r: Binary search only works on a sorted list; sort first or use linear search.
mistakes.w: Using binary search on an unsorted list.

mistakes.r: It starts by checking the middle item of the list.
mistakes.w: Saying binary search always starts at the first item.

mistakes.r: Use DIV to get a whole-number index: (0 + 11) DIV 2 = 5.
mistakes.w: Calculating mid with ordinary division and getting a decimal such as 5.5.

mistakes.r: Use low = mid + 1 or high = mid - 1 because the middle item has already been checked.
mistakes.w: Setting low = mid or high = mid after checking the middle.

mistakes.r: Linear search can be faster on small lists, if the target is near the start, or when the data is unsorted and only searched once.
mistakes.w: Saying linear search is always slower than binary search.

mistakes.r: It halves the remaining list each time; linear search checks one at a time.
mistakes.w: Saying binary search checks the items one at a time.

mistakes.r: The last index is list.length - 1; going further causes an index error.
mistakes.w: Looping a linear search to list.length.

mistakes.r: State that the search ends when the end of the list (linear) or low > high (binary) is reached and report 'not found'.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to say what happens when the item is not found.

mistakes.r: It is faster because it needs fewer comparisons, discarding half the data each time.
mistakes.w: Saying binary search is faster because the computer works faster.

summary: You must know how linear search and binary search work, be able to apply, trace, complete and write each in pseudocode, and compare them, including that binary search needs a sorted list but needs far fewer comparisons on large data. It matters because Paper 2 asks you to carry out searches by hand, spot errors and justify which algorithm suits a given data set.

terms.d: A set of steps used to find out whether a particular value is in a collection of data and, if so, where.
The value that the search is looking for; also called the search item.
A search that checks each item in the list in turn, from the start, until the target is found or the end is reached.
A search on a sorted list that repeatedly compares the target with the middle item and discards the half that cannot contain it.
A list arranged in order, such as ascending numbers or alphabetical text; this is required for binary search.
The position of an item in an array; the first item has index 0.
The middle position of the part of the list still being searched, found using (low + high) DIV 2.
The indexes of the first and last items that could still contain the target.
Integer division: the whole number of times one number goes into another, ignoring the remainder.
Checking whether an item equals, is less than, or is greater than the target.
The situation needing the fewest steps, e.g. the target is the first item in a linear search.
The situation needing the most steps, e.g. the target is last or missing.
Repeating a block of instructions using a loop.
A Boolean variable, such as found, used to record whether a condition has occurred.
How quickly an algorithm completes its task, such as the number of comparisons it needs.

worked.q: [4 marks] A sorted list contains 500 items. State the maximum number of comparisons needed by (a) a linear search and (b) a binary search.
steps: (a) In the worst case the target is last or missing, so every item is checked: 500.
(b) Each comparison halves what is left: 500, 250, 125, 62, 31, 15, 7, 3, 1. That is 8 halvings until 1 item remains, then 1 final comparison.
Check: 2^8 = 256 is less than 500 but 2^9 = 512 is at least 500, so 9 comparisons are enough.

worked.ans: Model answer: Binary search needs a sorted list (1) because it uses the order to discard half of the items at each step (1). The list [9, 3, 7, 1, 8] is not sorted, so the target could be in either half and binary search could miss it (1). A linear search should be used, as it checks each item in turn and does not need sorted data (1).
worked.q: [4 marks] The list [9, 3, 7, 1, 8] is stored in an array. Explain why a binary search is not suitable and say which search should be used.
steps: The list is not in order.
A binary search compares with the middle item and discards half the list based on whether the target is higher or lower.
With unsorted data you cannot tell which half contains the target, so the wrong half could be discarded.
A linear search checks every item in turn and works on unsorted data.
